Female Great sculpin Myoxocephalus polyacanthocephalus attain a maximum recorded total length of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters], a size that distinguishes this species as one of the larger members of the Cottidae family in the North Pacific. This ultimate length (80 centimeters) [Li = 80 centimeters] is typically reached only after many years of slow, sustained growth in the cold, productive waters of the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska. The corresponding maximum wet weight for females reaches approximately 5819 grams [Wwi = approximately 5819 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions that describe a strongly positive allometric relationship in this species. Such a substantial body mass reflects the extensive energy reserves required for producing large demersal egg masses and for surviving protracted periods of cold exposure during winter spawning seasons. The growth trajectory from a small pelagic larva to this large-bodied adult involves considerable ecological risk, as juvenile stages are vulnerable to a range of piscine and avian predators. The large ultimate size likely confers advantages in fecundity and in competitive interactions for desirable benthic shelter sites. Field surveys across the species range consistently support this maximum dimension of 80 centimeters [Li = 80 centimeters] as a reliable indicator of the species' life-history potential in undisturbed populations.

The onset of sexual maturity in Great sculpin is marked by the attainment of a total length of 56 centimeters [Lp = 56 centimeters], at which point females are capable of initiating vitellogenesis and participating in annual spawning aggregations. Body mass at this pubertal transition is estimated at 1892 grams [Wwp = 1892 grams], representing a substantial investment in somatic growth before the allocation of resources toward gamete production begins. This pubertal threshold is typically reached after several years of benthic juvenile development, during which individuals transition from a diet dominated by small crustaceans to one increasingly composed of larger demersal prey such as crabs and small teleosts. The length-based cue for maturity appears robust across the species' geographic distribution, although slight variations have been noted between populations in the Okhotsk Sea and those from the Gulf of Alaska. The relatively large size at first maturation compared to sympatric sculpin species suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes competitive ability and high fecundity over rapid generational turnover.

Reproductive output in Great sculpin has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate the thermal regime of their natural demersal spawning grounds. At a stable water temperature of 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C], females produce approximately 436 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 436 eggs per spawning event] throughout the protracted spawning season, with the daily rate sustained over many weeks of gamete release. This high fecundity is achieved through continuous oocyte recruitment and maturation, a pattern typical of batch-spawning cottids that deposit multiple demersal egg masses during a single reproductive period. The total reproductive output translates to roughly 159000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 159000 eggs per spawning event] with a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year] for a large, fully mature female, a value that underscores the substantial energetic investment this species makes in its offspring. Egg diameters average approximately 2.4 millimeters, producing large yolk-rich ova that confer a size advantage to the developing embryo during the prolonged incubation period in cold water. This reproductive strategy represents a classic trade-off between producing numerous small offspring versus fewer, more robustly provisioned larvae.

The earliest life stages of Great sculpin reflect the species' investment in large, well-provisioned eggs. The wet weight at birth, upon eclosion from the demersal egg, is approximately 0.0072 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0072 grams], a mass derived from the standard geometric conversion of an egg diameter of 2.4 millimeters based on data for the congener Myoxocephalus scorpius. This substantial hatchling mass compared to many other marine teleosts provides the newly emerged yolk-sac larva with considerable endogenous nutritional reserves, allowing it to survive for several weeks before the onset of exogenous feeding. The alevin remains in close association with the benthic substrate, where it absorbs its yolk sac and undergoes critical developmental changes including mouth gape opening, digestive tract differentiation, and initial swim bladder inflation. The provisioning strategy evident in the birth mass highlights a maternal investment pattern that improves early larval survival in the cold, food-limited environment typical of the species' high-latitude nursery habitats. Larval growth rates are strongly temperature-dependent, and hatchlings from eggs incubated at the lower end of the thermal range experience extended yolk-sac absorption periods.

Longevity data for Great sculpin in the wild indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] when maintained under natural thermal conditions averaging 3.2 °C [T = 3.2 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with the slow metabolic rates and delayed sexual maturation characteristic of large-bodied, cold-water cottids. Otolith-based age estimates from long-term mark-recapture studies in the Bering Sea confirm that individuals can persist for nearly two decades, with the oldest fish often exceeding 60 centimeters in total length and showing signs of reproductive senescence in their final years. The cold thermal environment slows the accumulation of physiological damage and oxidative stress, contributing to the remarkable longevity observed in this species relative to many other North Pacific demersal fishes. Life-history theory predicts that such prolonged lifespans evolve in environments where adult survival is high and unpredictable recruitment events favor repeated breeding opportunities across many seasons. The interplay between a slow growth trajectory, delayed maturity, and extended adult lifespan positions Myoxocephalus polyacanthocephalus as a classic example of a K-selected marine fish species in a highly seasonal, resource-predictable ecosystem.
